questions.q: Write the balanced chemical equation for the Rosenmund reduction of propanoyl chloride (CH₃CH₂COCl). Name the catalyst system and the gaseous byproduct.
questions.a: CH₃CH₂COCl + H₂ → CH₃CH₂CHO + HCl (g). Catalyst: Pd/BaSO₄ (poisoned with quinoline or sulfur). A wrong answer (e.g., writing CH₃CH₂CH₂OH as product) reveals the student does not understand that the reaction stops at the aldehyde due to catalyst poisoning; writing "Pd/C" or "Ni" shows confusion with standard hydrogenation catalysts that over-reduce.

questions.q: Why is the palladium catalyst in Rosenmund reduction supported on barium sulfate and poisoned with quinoline? Explain the consequence if unpoisoned Pd/C were used instead.
questions.a: BaSO₄ has low surface area, limiting Pd dispersion and thus reducing catalytic activity. Quinoline (or sulfur) selectively poisons the most active Pd sites responsible for aldehyde → alcohol reduction. If unpoisoned Pd/C were used, the aldehyde would be rapidly over-reduced to the primary alcohol (R-CH₂OH), defeating the purpose. A student who says "BaSO₄ increases surface area" or "quinoline speeds up the reaction" has the roles reversed.

questions.q: Predict the product(s) when each of the following acyl chlorides undergoes Rosenmund reduction: (i) CH₃COCl, (ii) C₆H₅COCl, (iii) ClCH₂CH₂COCl, (iv) HCOCl. Write structures.
questions.a: (i) CH₃CHO (ethanal), (ii) C₆H₅CHO (benzaldehyde), (iii) ClCH₂CH₂CHO (3-chloropropanal), (iv) HCOCl (formyl chloride) is unstable and decomposes to CO + HCl; Rosenmund reduction fails. A student who gives HCHO for (iv) ignores the instability of formyl chloride — a classic JEE trap. Writing CH₃CH₂OH for (i) shows over-reduction misunderstanding.

questions.q: Compare Rosenmund reduction with reduction of an ester using DIBAL-H at -78°C. Both give aldehydes. List two mechanistic differences and one practical advantage of each method.
questions.a: Mechanistic differences: (1) Rosenmund is heterogeneous catalytic hydrogenation (H₂/Pd) via surface adsorption; DIBAL-H is homogeneous hydride delivery via nucleophilic addition to carbonyl. (2) Rosenmund eliminates HCl; DIBAL-H forms a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate that requires aqueous workup. Practical: Rosenmund uses cheap H₂ gas and is scalable for industry; DIBAL-H allows low-temperature control for sensitive substrates and avoids HCl gas evolution. A student who claims both use "hydride reduction" confuses catalytic hydrogenation with hydride reagents.

questions.q: A student attempts Rosenmund reduction of CH₃(CH₂)₄COCl using Pd/BaSO₄ but forgets to add quinoline. The product mixture contains two organic compounds. Identify them and explain how you would separate them using a chemical test.
questions.a: Products: hexanal (CH₃(CH₂)₄CHO) and hexan-1-ol (CH₃(CH₂)₄CH₂OH). Separation: Add Tollens' reagent — hexanal gives Ag mirror (oxidation to carboxylate), hexan-1-ol does not react. Alternatively, NaHSO₃ addition forms crystalline bisulfite adduct with hexanal only. A student who says "distill them" ignores similar boiling points; one who says "Fehling's test" forgets aromatic aldehydes don't react (not relevant here but shows rote memorization).

questions.q: Design a two-step synthesis of 4-methylbenzaldehyde from toluene using only reactions covered in Class 12 NCERT. Specify reagents for each step. (Hint: Rosenmund reduction is step 2.)
questions.a: Step 1: Side-chain chlorination of toluene (Cl₂, hv) → 4-methylbenzyl chloride (p-ClCH₂-C₆H₄-CH₃) — but wait, that gives mixture. Better: Oxidation of p-xylene? Actually, NCERT teaches: toluene → (CrO₂Cl₂, then H₂O) → p-tolualdehyde (Etard) but that's direct. For Rosenmund route: Step 1: p-xylene (1,4-dimethylbenzene) → side-chain chlorination (Cl₂, hv) → p-(chloromethyl)benzyl chloride? No. Standard route: p-toluic acid → SOCl₂ → p-methylbenzoyl chloride → Rosenmund. But p-toluic acid from p-xylene oxidation (KMnO₄). So: Step 1: p-xylene + KMnO₄/Δ → p-toluic acid; then SOCl₂ → p-methylbenzoyl chloride. Step 2: Rosenmund reduction (H₂, Pd/BaSO₄, quinoline) → 4-methylbenzaldehyde. A student who writes "toluene + Cl₂/hv → benzyl chloride → Rosenmund" gets benzaldehyde, not 4-methylbenzaldehyde — revealing inability to plan regioselective synthesis.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Rosenmund reduction is the catalytic ______ of an acyl chloride (acid chloride) to an aldehyde using hydrogen gas over a palladium catalyst deposited on barium sulfate (Pd/BaSO₄), often poisoned with quinoline or sulfur to prevent over-reduction to the primary alcohol.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are in a pharmaceutical lab needing pure ______ for a synthesis — but direct oxidation of toluene gives benzoic acid, and reducing benzoic acid gives benzyl alcohol.
What is Rosenmund reduction? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Rosenmund reduction is the catalytic hydrogenation of an acyl chloride (acid chloride) to an aldehyde using hydrogen gas over a palladium catalyst deposited on barium sulfate (Pd/BaSO₄), often poisoned with quinoline or sulfur to prevent over-reduction to the primary alcohol.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Rosenmund reduction?
questions.a: Students often write the catalyst as "Pd/BaSO₄" but forget the poison (quinoline/sulfur), then claim the product is the alcohol because "hydrogenation reduces carbonyls to alcohols".

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) write the balanced chemical equation for Rosenmund reduction given any acyl chloride, (2) explain the role of BaSO₄ and the catalyst poison in controlling selectivity, and (3) predict the aldehyde product from a given acyl chloride and identify when this method is preferred over other aldehyde syntheses.
